answer:
**R-squared compares your squared error with a particular constant baseline.** Its denominator is the squared error from predicting the evaluation set's mean. A negative value means the model is worse than that baseline; it is mathematically valid. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html)

Take test targets (0,1,2). Their mean is 1 and total squared deviation is 2. Predictions (3,3,3) have squared error 9+4+1=14, giving $R^2=1-14/2=-6$. A large negative number is possible when predictions are very poor or the target varies very little.

For ordinary training-set least squares with an intercept, the fitted model can do at least as well as its intercept-only special case, so conventional training R-squared is nonnegative. That argument does not apply automatically to held-out data or to a model without an intercept.

**Adjusted R-squared penalizes extra predictors through degrees of freedom.** It can decrease when a new feature improves fit too little to justify the added parameter. However, it remains an in-sample formula under specific assumptions, not a substitute for validation or a universal complexity measure for arbitrary ML models. Report absolute error and baseline results, and handle a constant target explicitly because its denominator is zero.

**Technical details and references.**

Test $R^2$ is negative when squared prediction error exceeds the error of predicting that test set's mean. An intercept-free regression can also have negative conventional centered $R^2$ even in sample. A constant target makes the denominator zero, requiring an explicit convention. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html)

$$\bar R^2=1-(1-R^2)\frac{n-1}{n-p-1}$$

is the usual adjusted in-sample formula for $p$ predictors plus an intercept, when the denominator is positive. It penalizes additional predictors but is not a substitute for held-out validation and is not directly appropriate for arbitrary model complexity. Report absolute error, baseline comparison, and split design. A high $R^2$ on a nonstationary or leaked time series can be misleading.
